newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Key facts and figures about Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Key facts and figures about Chechnya.

text.p: Chechnya, where Aslan Maskhadov was inaugurated as president on Wednesday, has been a Russian region for nearly 140 years, but after a two-year war with Moscow, is set on independence.
Here are some key facts and figures about Chechnya.

TERRITORY: Some 15,000 sq km (5,800 sq miles) -- about half the size of Belgium or a shade bigger than Connecticut. Sitting on Russia's southern flank, it has an 80 km (50 mile) frontier with Georgia along the 5,000-metre (16,000-foot) Caucasus ridge.

POPULATION: Before the 1994-96 war, some 1.1 million people -- two-thirds of them ethnic Chechens and a quarter Russians. Ethnic Russians were concentrated in the capital, Grozny, where nearly 400,000 people lived in 1994 and some northern areas of Chechnya. There are no reliable data on casualties, but tens of thousands of civilians died in the fighting and hundreds of thousands fled. Many refugees are in the neighbouring regions of Dagestan, Ingushetia and North Ossetia but many, especially ethnic Russians, moved further afield.
Chechnya is a very much a clan society, some clans based in the mountains, some on the plains.

ECONOMY: Oil output flourished from the late 19th century but reserves are now scarce. Hopes of economic revival centre on rebuilding war-damaged refineries and earning money from a pipeline carrying Caspian reserves to the Black Sea. Official unemployment is estimated at up to 90 percent. But many Chechens work the land in extended families and receive cash from relatives in Russia and elsewhere. Moscow has promised aid but reconstruction of buildings wrecked in the war has barely begun.

HISTORY: The mountain people of Chechnya converted to Islam from the late 16th century. Two hundred years of sporadic war with Russia began when Christian Georgia agreed a union with Moscow in 1783, leaving the north Caucasus encircled. The Chechen Sheikh Mansour led a jihad or holy war in the 1780s but the fiercest fighting was in the 1817-64 Caucasus War. Russians coined the name "Chechen". Chechens call their nation Ichkeria. It was incorporated into the Russian empire in 1859. Grozny -- it means "Terrible" in Russian -- was founded in 1870.

In 1944, Soviet dictator Josef Stalin deported the entire Chechen people to the steppes of Central Asia, accusing them of aiding the German invaders, and many thousands died. In 1957 Nikita Khrushchev allowed the Chechens and their Ingush kin to return and established the Checheno-Ingush ethnic republic.

In October 1991, Soviet Air Force general Dzhokhar Dudayev stirred up protests against Grozny rulers and won 80 percent support in an election. He declared independence and then faced down a brief and bloodless military expedition from Moscow. Chechnya split from Ingushetia in June 1992 and began to earn a reputation in Russia as a haven for armed bandits and smugglers.

President Boris Yeltsin ordered troops into Chechnya on December 11, 1994. Badly-led troops met fierce resistance from determined guerrillas. Russia took Grozny and much of the Chechen plain by spring 1995 but never won full control.

In April 1996 Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev replaced Dudayev, who had been reported killed in a Russian rocket attack. Rebel forces infiltrated Grozny on August 6, 1996 and seized the city. Russia made peace on August 31, withdrawing its troops and leaving the Chechen sovereignty issue open for five years, but refusing to countenance secession.

ELECTIONS: Thirteen candidates vied for a five-year term in the January 27 presidential election. Maskhadov, a softly spoken former Sovier artillery colonel who headed the military resistance to the Rusian army, won easily, leaving prominent field commander Shamil Basayev and Yandarbiyev far behind.
All candidates vowed to do all they could to ensure Chechnya's independence from Moscow.

ARMED FORCES: There is no reliable information about the size of the rebel forces. About 5,000 guerrillas are believed to be under Maskhadov's command. But almost every grown-up man, and many teenagers in the region, is armed and traditionally seen as a potential warrior.
